    Dataset spatial operations¶

    pyramids wraps GDAL so that common raster transformations become a single method call on a Dataset. In this tutorial you load a digital-elevation model (DEM) of the Rhine river basin and walk through the three spatial operations you reach for most often: resampling to a coarser grid, reprojecting to a different coordinate reference system, and cropping one raster to the extent of another. Along the way you will see how each operation changes the grid's cell size, dimensions, and CRS.

    The spatial toolkit splits into two families: methods that transform the grid itself (live on ds.spatial) and methods that sample or summarise values at points and zones (live on ds.analysis):

    flowchart TB
    DS(("Dataset
    spatial operations"))
    DS --> T["transform the grid · ds.spatial
    resample · to_crs · align · crop"]
    DS --> S["sample & summarise · ds.analysis
    sample · extract · overlay · footprint"]

    This tutorial focuses on the grid transforms — resampling, reprojecting, and cropping.

    Load the data¶

    We import the Dataset class — the entry point for every raster in pyramids — and point at a GeoTIFF DEM of the Rhine basin. The path is relative to this notebook.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    # NBVAL_IGNORE_OUTPUT
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from pyramids.plot import ColorBar

%matplotlib inline

path = "../../../examples/data/dem/DEM5km_Rhine_burned_fill.tif"
    # NBVAL_IGNORE_OUTPUT from pyramids.dataset import Dataset from pyramids.plot import ColorBar %matplotlib inline path = "../../../examples/data/dem/DEM5km_Rhine_burned_fill.tif"

    Dataset.read_file opens the GeoTIFF through GDAL and returns a Dataset object; it references the file lazily rather than pulling all the pixels into memory.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    dataset = Dataset.read_file(path)
    dataset = Dataset.read_file(path)

    Printing a Dataset shows a summary of its geospatial metadata — corner, cell size, dimensions, EPSG code, band information, and no-data value — a quick way to sanity-check what you just loaded.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    print(dataset)
    print(dataset)
                Top Left Corner: (32239263.70388, 5756081.42235)
            Cell size: 5000.0
            Dimension: 125 * 93
            EPSG: 4647
            Number of Bands: 1
            Band names: ['Band_1']
            Band colors: {0: 'gray_index'}
            Band units: ['']
            Scale: [1.0]
            Offset: [0]
            Mask: -3.4028234663852886e+38
            Data type: float32
            File: ../../../examples/data/dem/DEM5km_Rhine_burned_fill.tif

    Dataset.plot renders one band as a map through cleopatra and returns the glyph object. A few options worth knowing:

    parameter meaning typical value
    band which band to draw (0-based) 0
    vmin / vmax clip the colour scale to this range 0, 30
    title figure title any string
    colorbar typed colour-bar spec e.g. ColorBar(label="Elevation(m)")
    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    dataset.plot(vmin=0, title="Rhine River Basin", colorbar=ColorBar(label="Elevation(m)"))
    dataset.plot(vmin=0, title="Rhine River Basin", colorbar=ColorBar(label="Elevation(m)"))
    Out[4]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x27275f2d400>

    The DEM shows the Rhine basin: higher elevations (bright) toward the mountainous south, descending to the low-lying north-west. This is the grid that every operation below will transform.

    Resampling¶

    Resampling changes the pixel size (spatial resolution) of a raster, recomputing its values onto a new grid. Coarser cells shrink the array and smooth out detail; finer cells enlarge it. Before resampling, let's confirm the raster's current cell size.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    print(f"Cell size: {dataset.cell_size}")
    print(f"Cell size: {dataset.cell_size}")
    Cell size: 5000.0

    resample recomputes the raster onto a new grid at the requested cell size and returns a new Dataset.

    parameter meaning typical value
    cell_size target pixel size in the raster's CRS units 8000 (metres)
    method interpolation used to fill the new cells "bilinear", "nearest", "cubic"

    Because we move from 5 km to 8 km cells, the output array is smaller and its detail is smoothed.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    dataset_8km = dataset.resample(cell_size=8000, method="bilinear")
    dataset_8km = dataset.resample(cell_size=8000, method="bilinear")

    Plot the resampled DEM to see the effect of the coarser grid.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    dataset_8km.plot(
    vmin=0,
    title="Rhine River Basin (resampled to 8 km)",
    colorbar=ColorBar(label="Elevation(m)"),
)
    dataset_8km.plot( vmin=0, title="Rhine River Basin (resampled to 8 km)", colorbar=ColorBar(label="Elevation(m)"), )
    Out[7]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x27276200550>

    Same basin, blockier pixels: each 8 km cell now aggregates an area the old 5 km cells resolved more finely. The overall elevation pattern is preserved while local detail is lost.

    Reprojecting¶

    Reprojection re-expresses the raster in a different coordinate reference system (CRS). The source DEM is in a projected metric CRS (EPSG:4647, ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N); we will convert it to geographic lon/lat degrees (EPSG:4326, WGS 84). First inspect the current CRS and dimensions.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    print(f"EPSG: {dataset.epsg}")
print(f"Coordinate reference system: {dataset.crs}")
print(f"Dataset dimensions: {dataset.shape}")
    print(f"EPSG: {dataset.epsg}") print(f"Coordinate reference system: {dataset.crs}") print(f"Dataset dimensions: {dataset.shape}")
    EPSG: 4647
Coordinate reference system: PROJCS["ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N (zE-N)",GEOGCS["ETRS89",DATUM["European_Terrestrial_Reference_System_1989",SPHEROID["GRS 1980",6378137,298.257222101004,AUTHORITY["EPSG","7019"]],AUTHORITY["EPSG","6258"]],PRIMEM["Greenwich",0],UNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433,AUTHORITY["EPSG","9122"]],AUTHORITY["EPSG","4258"]],PROJECTION["Transverse_Mercator"],PARAMETER["latitude_of_origin",0],PARAMETER["central_meridian",9],PARAMETER["scale_factor",0.9996],PARAMETER["false_easting",32500000],PARAMETER["false_northing",0],UNIT["metre",1,AUTHORITY["EPSG","9001"]],AXIS["Easting",EAST],AXIS["Northing",NORTH],AUTHORITY["EPSG","4647"]]
Dataset dimensions: (1, 125, 93)

    to_crs warps the grid into the target EPSG code and returns a brand-new Dataset. Because degrees and metres are different units, the cell size and dimensions change as part of the reprojection.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    reprojected_dataset = dataset.to_crs(4326)
    reprojected_dataset = dataset.to_crs(4326)

    Print the reprojected dataset. Note the EPSG is now 4326, the corner is expressed in degrees, and the cell size is a fraction of a degree.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    print(reprojected_dataset)
    print(reprojected_dataset)
                Top Left Corner: (5.210230290109742, 51.9554111793825)
            Cell size: 0.05475332958287695
            Dimension: 104 * 123
            EPSG: 4326
            Number of Bands: 1
            Band names: ['Band_1']
            Band colors: {0: 'gray_index'}
            Band units: ['']
            Scale: [1.0]
            Offset: [0.0]
            Mask: -3.4028234663852886e+38
            Data type: float32
            File:

    Plot the reprojected DEM.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    reprojected_dataset.plot(
    vmin=0,
    title="Rhine River Basin (reprojected to WGS 84)",
    colorbar=ColorBar(label="Elevation(m)"),
)
    reprojected_dataset.plot( vmin=0, title="Rhine River Basin (reprojected to WGS 84)", colorbar=ColorBar(label="Elevation(m)"), )
    Out[11]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x272775b4050>

    The map now carries lon/lat degree axes instead of metres, and the basin is subtly stretched relative to the UTM version — that distortion is exactly the warp from a projected grid to a geographic one.

    Cropping to another raster¶

    Cropping (clipping) trims a raster down to the extent of a second dataset — ideal for cutting a large product to a study area. Here we take a Europe-wide precipitation raster and clip it to the Rhine DEM. Both rasters must share a CRS before cropping, so we reproject the precipitation raster first. Let's load it.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    path = "../../../examples/data/geotiff/noah-precipitation-1979-europe.tif"
meteo_data = Dataset.read_file(path)
    path = "../../../examples/data/geotiff/noah-precipitation-1979-europe.tif" meteo_data = Dataset.read_file(path)

    Print its metadata: it is a 4-band daily-precipitation raster covering Europe at 0.5° resolution in WGS 84 (each band is one day).

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    print(meteo_data)
    print(meteo_data)
                Top Left Corner: (-5.0, 55.0)
            Cell size: 0.5
            Dimension: 25 * 40
            EPSG: 4326
            Number of Bands: 4
            Band names: ['Band_1', 'Band_2', 'Band_3', 'Band_4']
            Band colors: {0: 'gray_index', 1: 'undefined', 2: 'undefined', 3: 'undefined'}
            Band units: ['', '', '', '']
            Scale: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
            Offset: [0, 0, 0, 0]
            Mask: -9.969209968386869e+36
            Data type: float32
            File: ../../../examples/data/geotiff/noah-precipitation-1979-europe.tif

    Plot band 0 (the first day) to see the full European extent before cropping.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    array_glyph = meteo_data.plot(
    band=0,
    figsize=(10, 5),
    title="Noah daily Precipitation 1979-01-01",
    colorbar=ColorBar(label="Rainfall mm/day", length=0.85),
    vmax=30,
)
    array_glyph = meteo_data.plot( band=0, figsize=(10, 5), title="Noah daily Precipitation 1979-01-01", colorbar=ColorBar(label="Rainfall mm/day", length=0.85), vmax=30, )

    Rainfall covers the whole continent; the Rhine basin is just a small window inside this field.

    To crop against the DEM the two rasters must share a CRS, so reproject the precipitation raster from WGS 84 into the DEM's UTM CRS (EPSG:4647).

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    meteo_data_r = meteo_data.to_crs(4647)
    meteo_data_r = meteo_data.to_crs(4647)

    Plot the reprojected precipitation to confirm it is now on the same metric CRS as the DEM.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    meteo_data_r.plot(band=0)
    meteo_data_r.plot(band=0)
    Out[16]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x272773428b0>

    Same rainfall field, now on a UTM grid with axes in metres — matching the DEM's CRS.

    crop clips the precipitation raster to the DEM's bounding box, keeping only the cells that overlap the Rhine basin.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    rhine_meteo_data = meteo_data_r.crop(dataset)
    rhine_meteo_data = meteo_data_r.crop(dataset)

    Plot the cropped result.

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    rhine_meteo_data.plot(band=0)
    rhine_meteo_data.plot(band=0)
    Out[18]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x2727621b650>

    Only the rainfall cells over the Rhine basin remain — the raster has been reduced to the study area.

    Finally, echo the cropped dataset's full GDAL description to confirm its reduced size (10 × 14 cells) and its CRS.

    Copied!
